name: Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle
description: Master the Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle with expert finishing mechanics, grip sequences, and defensive strategies for this dominant back attack.
summary: The Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle is a blood choke applied from back control where the figure-four leg lock immobilizes the opponent's torso, freeing both arms to compress the carotid arteries for one of grappling's highest-percentage finishes.
overview:
The Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle combines the highest-percentage submission in grappling with the most secure form of back control. The body triangle's figure-four leg lock around the opponent's torso creates constant breathing restriction and prevents standard back escape sequences, giving the attacker extended time to systematically work through the choking sequence without concern for positional loss.

Unlike the standard RNC from hooks where the attacker must constantly manage leg positioning, the body triangle frees both arms entirely for neck attack. The locked legs cannot be cleared through hip escaping or hook removal, meaning the defender must first solve the triangle problem before addressing the choke — a two-layered defensive challenge that dramatically reduces escape success rates. The breathing restriction from the triangle also forces the defender to work urgently, often leading to defensive errors that expose the neck.

The finishing mechanics remain identical to the standard RNC — the choking arm slides under the chin with the bicep and forearm compressing both carotid arteries — but the body triangle provides a force multiplier. The squeeze from the legs restricts the defender's ability to expand their chest and generate the power needed for effective hand fighting. Competition data consistently shows that RNC attempts from body triangle convert at significantly higher rates than from standard hooks, making this one of the most feared finishing combinations in modern grappling.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate to 30 seconds with proper release

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper forearm placement
Carotid artery injury from excessive force

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training. Never snap or jerk the choke. Partner should have full awareness of pressure building.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (say 'tap' or make any verbal sound)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body or mat
Going limp or loss of consciousness
Any distress signal or unusual sound
release_protocol: Immediately release choking arm upon tap signal
Remove hooks and body triangle lock
Gently guide partner to side-lying recovery position
Monitor consciousness and breathing for 30 seconds
If partner was unconscious, keep them lying down until fully alert
Never allow unconscious partner to stand immediately
training_restrictions: Never use competition speed or intensity in drilling
Never apply the choke to the trachea or windpipe
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with both hands
Stop immediately if partner makes any distress sound
Never hold a choke past the tap for any reason
Beginners must practice with extremely slow progression only

variations_and_setups.description: Instead of the classic hand-behind-head figure-four configuration, clasp both palms together behind the opponent's neck. The interlocked hands create a direct compression path across both carotid arteries without needing the bicep cup connection.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent actively blocks the bicep cup connection by trapping your non-choking hand or when you need a faster lock from a partially secured choking arm position

variations_and_setups.description: Begin with a short choke or chin strap grip where the forearm presses across the jawline, using jaw pressure as a lever to force the chin open. Once the chin defense breaks, immediately slide the forearm deeper under the chin and transition to the standard RNC figure-four grip.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against opponents with strong chin tuck defense who prevent direct forearm entry under the chin

variations_and_setups.description: Use the non-choking arm to overhook and trap one of the opponent's defensive arms against their own body before threading the choking arm under the chin. This eliminates half their defensive capability and prevents the two-on-one grip defense.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent relies heavily on two-on-one wrist control defense and you need to remove one of their defensive hands from the equation

attacker.name: from Body Triangle Attacker
attacker.description: Finish the Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle with systematic hand fighting, coordinated squeeze pressure, and high-percentage grip configurations.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle represents the convergence of two dominant control systems — the mechanical lock of the body triangle and the arterial compression of the RNC. Your legs handle all positional retention through the figure-four lock around the torso, freeing both arms entirely for the systematic process of clearing defensive hands, sliding the choking arm under the chin, and securing the finishing grip. The breathing restriction from your triangle creates a ticking clock that forces your opponent to defend urgently, generating the openings you need to advance your choke. Patient hand fighting combined with strategic squeeze pulses is the hallmark of elite finishing from this position.
key_principles: Use the positional security of the body triangle to methodically strip defensive grips rather than rushing the choke — patience converts to finishes
Slide the choking forearm under the chin at an angle from the side rather than forcing it straight through the center defense
Time your leg squeeze pulses with arm advancement to overwhelm the defender's ability to address both threats simultaneously
Press your head against the side of opponent's head to prevent chin tucking and control their head angle throughout the sequence
Ensure the choking arm is deep enough that the blade of your forearm crosses both carotid arteries before committing to the finishing squeeze
Maintain constant chest-to-back connection throughout the hand fighting sequence to prevent any space creation that enables escape
setup_requirements: Secure body triangle with deep figure-four lock positioned around opponent's lower ribcage and diaphragm for maximum breathing restriction
Establish seatbelt grip or collar control with choking-side arm over the shoulder and control arm under the armpit
Position your head tight against the side of opponent's head to limit their ability to tuck chin and create defensive barriers
Keep hips on mat beside opponent providing stable base and maximum squeeze leverage to prevent rolling counters
Confirm at least one hand is positioned near opponent's collar line ready to begin systematic grip stripping

execution_steps.action: Establish dominant hand position from seatbelt
execution_steps.description: From body triangle with seatbelt control, use your choking-side hand to begin stripping opponent's defensive grip on your controlling arm. Pulse your leg squeeze to split their attention between defending the choke and managing breathing restriction, creating windows for grip advancement.

execution_steps.action: Clear the chin defense with head frame
execution_steps.description: With your non-choking hand, create a frame against opponent's forehead or jaw to tilt their head away from the choking side. Combine forearm pressure across the forehead with a squeeze pulse from the triangle to force them to choose between protecting chin or addressing breathing restriction.

execution_steps.action: Thread the choking arm under the chin
execution_steps.description: Slide your choking forearm under their chin at a slight angle from the side rather than attacking straight through the center. The blade of your forearm should cross the front of the throat with the crook of your elbow centered directly under the chin. Keep your elbow tight against their chest to prevent them from pulling the arm down.
execution_steps.timing: 2-4 seconds — commit decisively once the window opens

execution_steps.action: Secure the rear hand connection on bicep
execution_steps.description: Bring your non-choking hand behind their head and connect it to the bicep of your choking arm. Your palm should cup your own bicep while your choking hand grabs your opposite shoulder or bicep, creating the classic figure-four choking configuration that compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds — fast transition once forearm is seated

execution_steps.action: Set the head trap behind the skull
execution_steps.description: Place the back of your non-choking hand against the back of their skull, pushing their head forward into the choke. This eliminates the space they need to tuck their chin and creates forward pressure that increases the arterial compression on both carotid arteries.

execution_steps.action: Finish the choke with coordinated squeeze
execution_steps.description: Squeeze your elbows together while expanding your chest behind their head. Simultaneously pulse your body triangle squeeze to prevent any last-second escape attempts. The combined leg and arm pressure produces a tap within 3-5 seconds of the full lock being secured. Maintain steady progressive pressure without jerking or cranking.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds to tap with proper lock

execution_steps.action: Release upon tap and ensure partner safety
execution_steps.description: The instant you feel or hear a tap signal, immediately release your choking arm and open your body triangle. Guide your partner to a side-lying recovery position and monitor their consciousness and breathing for at least 30 seconds. Never hold the choke past the tap for any reason.

common_counters.counter: Two-on-one wrist control — opponent grabs choking wrist with both hands to stall advancement
common_counters.your_response: Pulse body triangle squeeze to force them to release one hand for breathing management, or switch attack angle to opposite side. Use your free hand to peel their grip finger by finger rather than fighting the full two-on-one directly.

common_counters.counter: Deep chin tuck with shoulder shrug — opponent buries chin to chest and raises shoulders to block forearm entry
common_counters.your_response: Use forehead frame with non-choking hand to tilt their head and open the chin angle. Alternatively, transition to short choke variation where forearm pressure across the jaw acts as a lever. The body triangle squeeze limits the power they can generate to maintain chin tuck.

common_counters.counter: Triangle clearing attempt — opponent redirects both hands to attack the figure-four leg lock at the ankle
common_counters.your_response: Immediately advance choking arm as their hands leave neck defense. Their triangle clearing attempt creates an undefended window for the choke. Increase squeeze pressure while committing the choking arm under the now-exposed chin.

common_counters.counter: Turn and face escape — opponent tries to rotate their body toward you to escape back exposure
common_counters.your_response: Follow the turn with your hips while maintaining chest connection. The body triangle prevents full rotation, and the turning motion often creates better choking angles. Use the momentum of their turn to advance the choking arm along their jawline.

common_errors.error: Rushing the choke before establishing proper arm position through hand fighting
common_errors.consequence: Choking arm gets trapped in defensive grips, wasting energy, telegraphing the attack, and allowing opponent to establish strong two-on-one defense
common_errors.correction: Use patient hand fighting and systematic grip stripping from the seatbelt before committing the choking arm — let the body triangle pressure create the openings

common_errors.error: Placing forearm directly across the trachea instead of angling across the carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Creates a painful air choke that is slow to finish, easier to defend, and risks serious tracheal damage including potential permanent injury
common_errors.correction: Angle the forearm blade across both sides of the neck with the crook of the elbow centered directly under the chin — the forearm should contact carotid arteries, not the windpipe

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's head before attempting to finish the choke
common_errors.consequence: Opponent tucks chin creating a barrier that prevents full arterial compression, stalling the choke and allowing them to reset defensive grips
common_errors.correction: Use the non-choking hand behind the head to push it forward into the choke before squeezing — the head trap eliminates the chin tuck defense

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arms only while neglecting body triangle coordination
common_errors.consequence: Reduced finishing power and allows opponent to focus entirely on hand defense without the distraction of breathing restriction, lowering conversion rate
common_errors.correction: Coordinate triangle squeeze pulses with arm attacks to divide opponent's defensive attention — the leg pressure creates the windows for arm advancement

common_errors.error: Loosening the body triangle lock while focusing exclusively on the choking sequence
common_errors.consequence: Creates escape opportunities that the defender exploits to clear the triangle and recover position, losing the dominant control that makes this finish so effective
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant triangle lock integrity throughout the choking sequence — the triangle is the foundation that enables the choke, never sacrifice leg position for arm advancement

common_errors.error: Choking arm positioned too shallow with forearm not fully across both carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Choke becomes a neck crank or partial compression that opponent can survive and defend, wasting the positional advantage and allowing recovery time
common_errors.correction: Ensure the blade of the forearm crosses both carotid arteries with the elbow crook centered under the chin before attempting to finish — if the arm is not deep enough, reset and re-enter

training_progressions.focus: Figure-four choking configuration and forearm placement
training_progressions.description: Practice the hand placement, bicep cup, and elbow positioning of the RNC grip from body triangle without resistance. Drill smooth transitions from seatbelt to choking position repeatedly on both sides. Focus on proper forearm angle across the carotid arteries.

training_progressions.focus: Systematic grip stripping against defensive hands
training_progressions.description: Partner holds defensive grips at 50% resistance. Practice clearing two-on-one defenses, chin tuck counters, and shoulder shrug bypasses using technique rather than strength. Develop timing for when to commit the choking arm through the opening.

training_progressions.focus: Leg squeeze and arm attack coordination
training_progressions.description: From established body triangle, practice timing triangle squeeze pulses with arm advancement. Partner defends at 70% resistance. Focus on using leg pressure to create choking windows and splitting the defender's attention between upper and lower body threats.

Start from body triangle with partner defending at full resistance. Three-minute rounds focused exclusively on finishing the RNC. Track success rate, identify patterns in failed attempts, and develop ability to chain between grip variations when primary attack is defended.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Rear Naked Choke target and why is forearm placement critical?
flashcards.answer: The RNC targets both carotid arteries and jugular veins on either side of the neck. The choking forearm compresses one side while the bicep compresses the other, with the crook of the elbow positioned under the chin. This bilateral compression cuts blood flow to the brain, causing unconsciousness within 5-10 seconds. The forearm must angle across the carotid arteries and never directly compress the trachea, as tracheal pressure creates a dangerous air choke with risk of permanent injury.

flashcards.question: What indicators confirm the choke is properly positioned before you commit to the finishing squeeze?
flashcards.answer: The blade of your forearm should contact both sides of the neck with equal pressure. The crook of your elbow should sit directly under the chin, not shifted to either side. Your non-choking hand should be behind their head with palm cupping your own bicep. You should feel firm contact against the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck. If the forearm is pressing against the front of the throat or windpipe, you must reposition before squeezing.

plausible: Forearm firm on one side only

flashcards.question: How does the body triangle change finishing mechanics compared to a standard hooks-based RNC?
flashcards.answer: The body triangle eliminates the need for active leg management, freeing both arms entirely for the choking sequence. The constant breathing restriction creates urgency that forces defensive errors and limits the power the defender can generate for hand fighting. The locked legs prevent hip escaping and turning, which are the primary escape mechanisms from standard hook-based back control. This results in significantly higher finishing rates and longer uninterrupted choking sequences.
flashcards.answer_line: Frees arms, locks out hip escape

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks their chin aggressively and you cannot thread the forearm directly — what grip adjustment breaks through?
flashcards.answer: Attack from the side by sliding the choking hand along the jawline from the ear rather than forcing through the center. Use the non-choking hand to frame against the forehead, tilting the head away from the choking side. Alternatively, use a short choke variation where forearm pressure across the jaw acts as a lever to pry the chin open, then transition to standard RNC once the defense breaks. The body triangle squeeze limits the defender's ability to maintain a strong chin tuck under sustained pressure.
flashcards.answer_line: Slide in from ear, frame forehead

trap: Let go and reset both hooks

flashcards.question: What is the proper release protocol when your partner taps to this choke?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release the choking arm upon any tap signal — verbal, physical hand tap, or foot tap. Then unlock and remove the body triangle entirely. Guide your partner to a side-lying recovery position and monitor their consciousness and breathing for at least 30 seconds. If they lost consciousness at any point, keep them lying down until fully alert and never allow them to stand immediately. Any delay in release risks unnecessary injury.

plausible: Let them stand up right away
trap: Hold choke a few extra seconds

flashcards.question: At what point during the choke setup is the defender effectively past the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: Once the choking arm is fully threaded under the chin with the elbow crook centered and the non-choking hand is secured behind the head on the bicep, escape from body triangle becomes nearly impossible. The combined leg immobilization and locked choking configuration typically produces a tap within 3-5 seconds. The critical transition point is when the choking hand connects to the opposite shoulder — at that moment, hand defense alone cannot prevent the finish.

flashcards.question: What common finishing error turns a blood choke into a potentially dangerous tracheal compression?
flashcards.answer: Placing the forearm directly across the trachea instead of angling it across the carotid arteries creates an air choke that compresses the windpipe. This is both less effective as a finishing technique and more dangerous, as tracheal damage can result in serious injury requiring weeks of recovery or potentially permanent damage. The correction is ensuring the blade of the forearm contacts both sides of the neck with the crook of the elbow positioned directly under the chin.

flashcards.question: How do you coordinate body triangle pressure with choke attempts to maximize finishing effectiveness?
flashcards.answer: Use pulsing leg squeezes timed with arm advancement to split the defender's attention. When you strip a defensive grip, simultaneously pulse the triangle to prevent them from resetting their hands. During the final squeeze, coordinate leg and arm pressure together for maximum force multiplication. The defender cannot effectively address both breathing restriction and neck defense simultaneously, so alternating pressure between upper and lower body creates consistent advancement windows.

plausible: Squeeze legs only at the end
trap: Release legs to focus on arms

defender.name: from Body Triangle Defender
defender.description: Defend the Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle with chin protection strategies, hand fighting sequences, and systematic escape methods from back control.
defender.overview: Defending against the Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle is among the most demanding defensive scenarios in grappling because you must address two simultaneous threats — the arterial compression of the choke and the breathing restriction of the body triangle. The locked legs prevent standard back escapes while your opponent's arms systematically work to clear your defensive grips and thread the choking arm under your chin. Successful defense requires immediate chin protection, disciplined hand fighting to prevent the choking arm from advancing, and systematic work to either stall the attack long enough to clear the triangle or create enough positional disruption to escape to a less dangerous position. The breathing restriction adds a time pressure element that demands calm, measured technique rather than panicked scrambling.
key_principles: Chin protection is the first and constant priority — keep chin tucked with at least one hand defending the neck at all times throughout the position
Fight the setup rather than the locked choke — preventing the choking arm from threading under the chin is far more achievable than escaping a fully locked RNC
Manage breathing under compression by taking controlled chest breaths rather than fighting for full diaphragmatic expansion that the triangle prevents
Never remove both hands from neck defense simultaneously — address the body triangle with one hand while maintaining neck protection with the other
Address threats in priority order: protect neck first, manage breathing second, work on triangle clearing third
Maintain mental composure under physical stress — accept the breathing discomfort and work methodically rather than panicking into energy-wasting scrambles
recognition_cues: Opponent's forearm begins sliding along your jawline or collar area, indicating the choking arm is advancing toward your neck
Increased body triangle squeeze pressure signals the attacker is about to commit to a choke attempt, using leg pressure to distract from arm advancement
Non-choking hand frames against your forehead or jaw attempting to tilt your head and break your chin tuck defense
One of your defensive grips is stripped from the collar area while opponent maintains seatbelt or upper body control
Head pressure from behind — opponent presses their head firmly against yours to control your head angle and prevent chin defense

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one wrist control on the choking arm to stall advancement
defensive_options.when_to_use: Early in the sequence when opponent's choking hand begins advancing toward your neck from the seatbelt position
defensive_options.if_successful: Stalls the choke and forces opponent to reset their entire hand fighting sequence, buying time for triangle clearing
defensive_options.risk: Committing both hands to the wrist means if opponent breaks free or switches sides, your neck is momentarily undefended

defensive_options.action: Deep chin tuck with shoulder shrug to block forearm entry under the chin
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you feel the choking forearm beginning to slide toward or under your chin from any angle
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the choking arm from achieving proper position across the carotid arteries, maintaining defensive barrier
defensive_options.risk: Opponent uses head frame to tilt your chin open or switches to short choke variation that uses jaw pressure as a lever

defensive_options.action: One-handed triangle clearing while maintaining neck defense with the other hand
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you have successfully stalled the choke attempt and have a window to address the leg lock
defensive_options.if_successful: Breaks the body triangle figure-four lock, removing both the breathing restriction and the positional security that enables the choke
defensive_options.risk: Redirecting one hand to triangle clearing reduces neck defense, creating a window for the choking arm to advance

defensive_options.action: Turn into opponent with hip escape after disrupting the choking sequence
defensive_options.when_to_use: After successfully stalling the choke and when opponent overcommits to a grip break or adjusts their upper body position
defensive_options.if_successful: Fully escapes back control and recovers to closed guard, neutralizing both the choke threat and body triangle
defensive_options.risk: If body triangle is still fully locked, the turning motion may increase squeeze pressure and worsen the breathing restriction

escape_paths: Clear the body triangle figure-four lock by attacking the ankle behind the knee, then turn into opponent to recover half guard or closed guard
Strip the choking grips, create space by bridging and turning, and stand up in base to break the position entirely
Stall the choke with two-on-one wrist control while systematically working the triangle clear with your free hand and hip movement

favorable_outcomes.how: Clear the body triangle by attacking the figure-four lock at the ankle, use the space created to turn your hips and face the opponent, recovering to closed guard where neither the choke nor the body triangle can be maintained

Successfully defend all choke attempts through disciplined chin tuck and hand fighting, forcing the attacker to reset their choking sequence while you maintain defensive position and work incrementally toward clearing the triangle

common_errors.error: Panicking from breathing restriction and using explosive energy to scramble without technical precision
common_errors.consequence: Depletes oxygen faster under already restricted breathing conditions, leads to exhaustion and mental defeat, and creates defensive gaps the attacker exploits for the choke
common_errors.correction: Accept the breathing restriction as manageable discomfort, take controlled chest breaths, and work with measured technique at a sustainable pace

common_errors.error: Reaching back to attack the body triangle with both hands simultaneously
common_errors.consequence: Completely exposes the neck to the choking arm with zero defensive resistance, leading to immediate choke lock that cannot be escaped
common_errors.correction: Never remove both hands from neck defense at the same time — address the triangle with one hand while maintaining neck protection with the other throughout the clearing sequence

common_errors.error: Attempting to fight a fully locked RNC instead of preventing the setup
common_errors.consequence: Once the RNC is fully locked with the hand behind the head and body triangle preventing hip movement, escape probability drops below 5% — fighting a locked choke wastes the final seconds before unconsciousness
common_errors.correction: Focus all defensive energy on preventing the choking arm from threading under the chin — hand fight the setup aggressively rather than trying to strip a completed choke

common_errors.error: Extending the neck and lifting the chin trying to create breathing space
common_errors.consequence: Exposes the carotid arteries and lengthens the neck, making it significantly easier for the attacker to slide the forearm into optimal choking position
common_errors.correction: Keep chin tucked tight to chest at all times, compressing the neck to create the shortest possible distance for the attacker's forearm to travel

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that a Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle is being actively set up?
flashcards.answer: Key recognition cues include feeling the opponent's forearm sliding along your jawline or collar area, a sudden increase in body triangle squeeze pressure that signals an imminent choking attempt, the non-choking hand framing against your forehead to break your chin tuck, and the stripping of your defensive grips from the collar area. The body triangle squeeze often intensifies immediately before the choking arm commits, as the attacker uses leg pressure to distract from the arm advancement.

plausible: Only watch for hand on collar

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the Rear Naked Choke from Body Triangle during training?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel the choking arm fully lock under your chin with the opponent's hand secured behind your head on the bicep. From body triangle, escape from a locked RNC is nearly impossible because the legs prevent the hip movement needed for any escape technique. The 3-5 second window to unconsciousness from a properly applied blood choke is not enough time to execute an escape. Use any tap method available — verbal, hand tap on opponent or mat, or foot tap on mat. Tapping early preserves your safety and allows more productive training.
flashcards.answer_line: Tap when arm locks under chin

plausible: Wait until vision starts to blur
trap: Try to escape once it's locked

flashcards.question: What defensive options remain when the choking arm is partially threaded under your chin?
flashcards.answer: Use both hands to grab the choking wrist or forearm and pull it down away from your neck while tucking your chin as tightly as possible. Try to turn your head toward the choking arm side to reduce the angle of attack and prevent further advancement. If you create any space, immediately return to a strong two-handed defensive position on the collar area. This is the critical window — if the arm advances further and the opponent secures the bicep cup, the choke becomes locked and escape probability drops dramatically.
flashcards.answer_line: Pull arm down, tuck chin, turn in

plausible: Turn head away from choking arm
Push off with both hands on hips
trap: Let go and clear the triangle

flashcards.question: Why is addressing the body triangle before the choke generally the wrong priority order?
flashcards.answer: The body triangle is uncomfortable but not immediately finishing — it restricts breathing but does not cause unconsciousness on its own. The RNC causes unconsciousness within 5-10 seconds of full application. Prioritizing the triangle over neck defense redirects both hands away from your throat, creating an undefended window that the attacker will exploit to lock the choke. The correct order is always neck defense first, breathing management second, and triangle clearing as a tertiary objective when the choke is not actively being advanced.

trap: Use both hands to clear triangle

flashcards.question: What is the safest defensive hand position to maintain throughout body triangle back control?
flashcards.answer: Keep at least one hand defending your neck at all times by positioning it on your collar, across your throat, or controlling the opponent's choking forearm. The second hand can work on grip fighting, clearing the triangle, or creating frames, but must return to neck defense whenever the opponent advances their choking attempt. The golden rule is never having both hands below your chin simultaneously — this creates an unrecoverable window for the choking arm to lock in position.
flashcards.answer_line: One hand always guards the neck

plausible: Both hands grip fighting is fine
trap: Use both hands to strip triangle

flashcards.question: What body angle or positioning minimizes the body triangle's effectiveness while you work on escape?
flashcards.answer: Turn your body slightly toward the locked leg side of the triangle, which is the side where the opponent's ankle is tucked behind their knee. This reduces the squeeze angle and decreases the surface area of compression on your ribcage, making breathing easier. Keep your hips slightly angled rather than flat, as this creates less optimal squeezing geometry for the attacker. Avoid turning away from the triangle leg as this often increases compression and gives the attacker better choking angles on the exposed side of your neck.

plausible: Turn away from the triangle leg
trap: Arch back to open the ribcage

flashcards.question: Your opponent transitions from the standard RNC attempt to applying forearm pressure directly on your jaw — how do you respond?
flashcards.answer: When the attacker uses jaw pressure as a lever to pry your chin open, resist the temptation to open your mouth or lift your chin to relieve the discomfort. Clamp your jaw shut, tuck your chin even tighter to your chest, and use both hands to control the forearm applying pressure. The jaw pressure is uncomfortable but not dangerous in itself — the danger comes from capitulating and allowing the forearm to slide under your chin to the neck. Maintain your chin defense through the discomfort rather than giving up the neck to relieve jaw pressure.
flashcards.answer_line: Clamp jaw, tuck chin, control arm

plausible: Lift chin to ease the pressure
trap: Give the neck to ease jaw pain

flashcards.question: When is the only safe moment to commit both hands to clearing the body triangle lock?
flashcards.answer: The only safe time to use both hands on the triangle is when the attacker has fully committed both of their arms to a position that is not threatening your neck — for example, when they are adjusting their upper body grips or transitioning between control configurations. If either of the attacker's hands is near your collar or neck area, you must keep at least one hand defending. Even during a brief two-handed triangle clearing attempt, you must immediately return one hand to neck defense if you feel any advancement of the choking arm toward your chin.
flashcards.answer_line: When both attacker hands are clear

trap: Both hands off, ignore arm moves

training_progressions.focus: Understanding when to tap and recognizing choke stages
training_progressions.description: Partner applies slow, controlled RNC from body triangle at 30% speed. Practice recognizing the point of no return and tapping before pressure becomes dangerous. Build awareness of the difference between arterial compression sensation and air choke discomfort.

training_progressions.focus: Preventing the choke setup through grip defense
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts to thread choking arm at 50% speed with body triangle locked. Practice two-on-one wrist control, chin tuck maintenance, and systematic grip fighting patterns. Focus on preventing the arm from advancing rather than escaping a locked choke.

training_progressions.focus: Addressing body triangle while maintaining neck defense
training_progressions.description: Start in body triangle with partner alternating between choke attempts and squeeze pressure at 60% intensity. Practice one-handed triangle clearing while maintaining neck defense with the other hand. Build the coordination to address both threats without compromising either defense.

training_progressions.focus: Complete defensive sequences against increasing resistance
training_progressions.description: Three-minute rounds starting from body triangle with partner attacking at progressive intensity. Practice complete defensive sequences from initial chin protection through choke defense to triangle clearing and guard recovery. Track survival time and escape success rate across sessions.

clips.title: Defending the Figure 4 from the Back
